regulated_party: Courts and law enforcement agencies offering UAV-derived evidence (public agency only)
regulated_activity: Introducing information obtained from UAV use as evidence in a criminal or civil proceeding
requirement_type: Evidentiary admissibility condition (search warrant, or otherwise consistent with state and federal law)
permit_or_approval_required: Search warrant required for admissibility (not a use-permit)
summary: Provides that information obtained through the use of an unmanned aerial vehicle is not admissible as evidence in a criminal or civil proceeding unless obtained pursuant to the authority of a search warrant, or otherwise obtained in a manner consistent with state and federal law. Enacted in 2014 as part of House File 2289 (2014 Acts, ch. 1111, §2), alongside §321.492B (IA-002). This is an evidentiary rule; it does not itself authorize, restrict, or license UAV operation by any person or agency, and does not directly regulate private/commercial UAS operators.
verification_status: Full current section text verified directly against the Iowa Legislature's official Iowa Code PDF mirror (legis.iowa.gov); the 2014 enactment (2014 Acts, ch. 1111, §2) is confirmed in the section's own history note and was cross-checked against the enrolled/chaptered text of House File 2289.
notes: Companion provision to §321.492B (IA-002); both originate from the same 2014 enacting act (H.F. 2289 / 2014 Acts ch. 1111), which also directed an uncodified Department of Public Safety study (Sec. 3) on whether Iowa's criminal code should be further modified for UAS — a study that appears to have informed the later, separate 2018 (§719.9) and 2024/2025 (ch. 715E) enactments. See IA-007 for a related citation-discrepancy finding concerning this same 2014 act.

source_title: Remotely Piloted Aircraft — Intrusion, Surveillance, Injunctive Relief, and Exceptions
citation: Iowa Code ch. 715E, §§715E.1-715E.6 (2024 Acts, ch. 1131, §§1-6; amended by 2024 Acts, ch. 1154, §§21-22; further amended by 2025 Acts, ch. 56, §§1-10)
uas_topic: Private-property UAV intrusion/surveillance restriction (homestead and farmstead), with an express commercial/agricultural-use exemption
regulated_party: Any person operating a remotely piloted aircraft (private/commercial operators); express exceptions for the consenting owner/lessee, government agencies, public utilities, and railroad companies
regulated_activity: Knowingly controlling the flight of a remotely piloted aircraft over another's homestead, or over a farmstead within 400 feet of a farm animal, farm equipment, or farm structure, without consent
requirement_type: Prohibition (simple misdemeanor for intrusion; serious misdemeanor for surveillance with a surveillance device; enhanced on repeat conviction), plus a civil injunctive-relief remedy for the property owner/lessee
permit_or_approval_required: N/A (owner/lessee consent is the operative exception, not an agency permit)
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — but subject to an express statutory exemption
summary: Sections 715E.3 (intrusion) and 715E.4 (surveillance) make it an offense to knowingly fly a remotely piloted aircraft over another's 'homestead' (a principal residence, outside city limits, plus up to 400 feet of surrounding land) or over a 'farmstead' (at least 40 contiguous acres used for farming, generating at least $15,000 annually in farm-commodity sales, per the 2025 amendment) within 400 feet of a farm animal, farm equipment, or farm structure, without the owner's or lessee's consent. Surveillance (a flight equipped with a device capturing an identifiable image, sound, or data) is a serious misdemeanor; intrusion alone is a simple misdemeanor; both are enhanced on repeat conviction. Section 715E.5 allows the property owner or lessee to petition for a temporary injunction (up to two years, renewable) plus costs and attorney fees, and generally requires destruction of unlawfully obtained recordings, subject to defined ownership-interest exceptions. Section 715E.6 exempts, among others, a person operating 'for a commercial or agricultural use in compliance with Federal Aviation Administration regulations, authorizations, or exemptions,' a person flying more than 400 feet above the earth's surface, and government, public-utility, and railroad-company operators. Originally enacted in 2024 (H.F. 572, 2024 Acts ch. 1131) protecting only a narrower 'secured farmstead' (an animal feeding operation plus 400 feet); broadened in 2025 (S.F. 491, 2025 Acts ch. 56) to the current 40-acre/$15,000 'farmstead' definition.
verification_status: Full current text of §§715E.1 through 715E.6 verified directly against the Iowa Legislature's official Iowa Code PDF mirrors for each individual section; the 2024 original enactment (H.F. 572, 2024 Acts ch. 1131, signed May 3, 2024) and the 2025 amendment (S.F. 491, 2025 Acts ch. 56, signed May 6, 2025) are confirmed in each section's own history notes and independently corroborated by Iowa Capital Dispatch's contemporaneous legislative reporting (March 17, 2025) on S.F. 491's Senate passage.
notes: AEC-CRITICAL FINDING: §715E.6(2) expressly exempts a person operating a remotely piloted aircraft 'for a commercial or agricultural use in compliance with federal aviation administration regulations, authorizations, or exemptions' from both the intrusion and surveillance offenses, and §715E.6(6) separately exempts any flight conducted more than 400 feet above the earth's surface. Together these are the most operationally significant provisions of this chapter for FAA Part 107 commercial AEC operators; unlike some other states' privacy statutes reviewed in this program, Iowa's homestead/farmstead protections do not appear to reach compliant commercial UAS operations on their face, though the exemption's precise scope (e.g., a commercial flight for a non-agricultural purpose, such as a utility-corridor survey, that nonetheless passes within 400 feet of a farmstead) has not been construed by any Iowa court or agency as of this research date.

source_title: Use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle — Prohibitions (Correctional and Detention Facilities)
uas_topic: Correctional/detention-facility UAV restriction, with an express commercial-use exemption
regulated_party: Any person (private/commercial operators); law enforcement agencies and facility-permission holders excepted
regulated_activity: Operating a UAV knowing it is operating in, on, or above a county jail, municipal holding facility, secure juvenile detention facility, community-based correctional facility, or Iowa Department of Corrections institution, or its contiguous surrounding grounds
requirement_type: Prohibition (class "D" felony), subject to a law-enforcement exception and a facility-authority-permission exception
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — permission from the authority in charge of the facility (no standardized statewide permit process)
commercial_operator_relevance: Yes — but subject to an express statutory exemption
summary: Makes it a class "D" felony to knowingly operate a UAV in, on, or above a covered facility (county jail, municipal holding facility, secure juvenile detention facility, community-based correctional facility, or a Department of Corrections institution) or its contiguous surrounding grounds, unless the UAV is operated by a law enforcement agency or the operator has permission from the authority in charge of the facility. Subsection 3 expressly provides that the section 'does not apply to an unmanned aerial vehicle while operating for commercial use in compliance with federal aviation administration regulations, authorizations, or exemptions.'
verification_status: Full current section text verified directly against the Iowa Legislature's official Iowa Code PDF mirror; the 2018 enactment (2018 Acts, ch. 1168, §20) is confirmed in the section's own history note.
notes: Notably broader commercial exemption than the correctional-facility statutes found in some other states in this program (contrast Indiana's IN-004, which requires facility-head authorization for any UAV-delivered item with no comparable blanket commercial-use exception). AEC firms conducting FAA Part 107-compliant commercial inspection or mapping work near an Iowa correctional facility should nonetheless confirm the exemption's applicability and coordinate with the facility in advance, given the felony penalty and 'knowing' mens rea.

issuing_authority: Iowa General Assembly / Iowa Department of Natural Resources
source_title: Hunting from Aircraft Prohibited — DNR Construction Applying the Statute to Drones
citation: Iowa Code §481A.120 (most recently amended 2022 Acts, ch. 1032, §83); construed to include drones in the Iowa DNR's "2025-26 Iowa Hunting, Trapping & Migratory Game Bird Regulations" official guidance booklet
source_type: Binding law or regulation, supplemented by official agency guidance
effective_date: Unknown original enactment (pre-1950 Iowa Code); most recently amended 2022
binding_level: Binding (statute); Advisory guidance (DNR booklet's construction of "aircraft" to include drones)
regulated_activity: Intentionally killing, wounding, attempting to kill or wound, or pursuing an animal, fowl, or fish from or with an aircraft in flight (or a snowmobile)
summary: Iowa Code §481A.120 prohibits intentionally killing, wounding, attempting to kill or wound, or pursuing an animal, fowl, or fish from or with an 'aircraft in flight' or a snowmobile. The statutory text itself does not define 'aircraft' to include an unmanned aerial vehicle or drone. The Iowa DNR's own '2025-26 Iowa Hunting, Trapping & Migratory Game Bird Regulations' booklet expressly states, under a 'DRONES' heading, that 'drones are considered aircraft by the U.S. Federal Government' and that 'the use of drones while hunting is not allowed,' and separately restates the §481A.120 prohibition as reaching hunting 'from or with an aircraft or drone in flight.' The booklet itself states it is 'not a complete list of all hunting regulations or laws, nor is it a legal document.'
verification_status: Statutory text of §481A.120 verified directly against the Iowa Legislature's official Iowa Code PDF mirror. The DNR's construction of 'aircraft' to include drones was verified directly against the current (2025-26 season) official DNR hunting-regulations PDF (iowadnr.gov), but that booklet is agency guidance rather than a codified rule or administrative regulation, and it expressly disclaims being a complete or legally authoritative statement of hunting law.
notes: No separate Iowa Administrative Code rule (comparable to, e.g., Indiana's IC 14-22-6-16) was located that codifies a UAV-specific hunting restriction; the drone-inclusive reading rests on the DNR's own guidance document construing the existing 'aircraft' statute, not on UAV-specific statutory or rule text. Relevance to AEC work is limited to firms conducting wildlife-survey or agricultural-monitoring UAS work in or near hunting seasons; this should not be confused with a general DNR-land no-fly rule (see IA-007 — no such rule was located).

effective_date: Unknown original enactment (Code 1993 recodification of prior ch. 114)
binding_level: Binding (general licensing framework only — no UAS-specific rule or guidance identified)
uas_topic: General professional-licensing competency for photogrammetric/geodetic survey methods (no UAS-specific rule or guidance located)
regulated_party: Licensed professional land surveyors; persons performing survey-grade measurement of property lines, boundaries, or geodetic positions
regulated_activity: Practicing land surveying — including geodetic surveying and creation/modification of GIS/LIS data relative to boundary determination — without licensure
requirement_type: Licensure requirement, subject to the chapter's other provisions (e.g., the engineering-survey carve-out in §542B.2(5))
permit_or_approval_required: License (professional land surveyor) generally required for the practice of land surveying as defined
summary: Iowa Code §542B.2(10) defines the 'practice of land surveying' to include consultation, investigation, evaluation, planning, mapping, and interpreting reliable scientific measurements relative to property boundaries, including geodetic surveying for precise positioning of permanent land survey monuments and the creation or modification of electronic/computerized data (including land information systems and geographic information systems) relative to those activities. The definition is method-neutral and does not reference photogrammetry, LiDAR, or UAS by name. No standalone rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ from the Iowa Engineering and Land Surveying Examining Board or the Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing specifically addressing UAS-derived photogrammetric or LiDAR mapping products was located during this research pass.
verification_status: Full current section text verified directly against the Iowa Legislature's official Iowa Code PDF mirror. The Board's public rule and FAQ pages (dial.iowa.gov, rules.iowa.gov) were reviewed for UAS-specific guidance; none was located, but the search was not exhaustive of every Board meeting minute or informal advisory the Board may have issued.
notes: Matches the general framework-only pattern flagged for other states in this program (see, e.g., Indiana IN-009): this is not itself UAS-specific guidance. Whether a UAS-derived deliverable falls inside licensed practice under §542B.2(10) is fact-specific; recommend direct inquiry to the Iowa Engineering and Land Surveying Examining Board (via dial.iowa.gov) before relying on this citation for a specific deliverable.

summary: No Iowa Governor executive order, Iowa Attorney General opinion, or Iowa appellate/Supreme Court decision directly addressing UAS was located. No Iowa-specific state-agency UAS procurement, approved-manufacturer, or country-of-origin restriction beyond the federal American Security Drone Act framework was located. No statewide statute preempting local UAS ordinances was located; the Iowa League of Cities' own member guidance (a non-authoritative advisory resource) advises cities to consult the FAA before adopting a drone ordinance, and no Iowa city is reported to have adopted a standalone drone ordinance. Iowa DNR's state-park/recreation-area administrative rule on public-use restrictions (571 IAC 61.10) was reviewed directly in full and contains no aircraft- or UAV-specific provision. The Iowa DOT's 'Uncrewed Aircraft Systems' webpage links to FAA resources (Part 107 certification, B4UFLY, a controlled-airspace map, and a waiver webinar series) but imposes no independent state requirement of its own. Iowa's critical-infrastructure sabotage statute (Iowa Code §§716.11-.12) was reviewed and contains no UAS-specific text; it reaches a UAV only in the rare case where the aircraft is the instrument of an actual, overt sabotage act, and is excluded from this register under the project's non-UAS scope gate. CITATION-DISCREPANCY FINDING: numerous secondary drone-law aggregator sites describe a current Iowa Code §708C.1 imposing a UAV weaponization ban, a state-agency image-capture/search-warrant regime, and related legislative-reporting requirements. Direct review of the enrolled/chaptered text of the 2014 enacting act (House File 2289, approved May 23, 2014, published as 2014 Acts ch. 1111) shows the Iowa Senate struck the bill's proposed new Chapter 708C — including the weaponization ban and a companion amendment to the stalking statute, §708.11 — before passage; only §321.492B (IA-002), §808.15 (IA-001), and an uncodified Department of Public Safety study directive were actually enacted. A direct query of the Iowa Legislature's current (2026) Code section listing for chapter 708C returned zero sections, confirming the chapter does not exist in current Iowa law.
verification_status: Enrolled/chaptered bill text of House File 2289 (2014 Acts ch. 1111) retrieved from a legislative-tracking mirror (legiscan.com) hosting the official Iowa Legislature bill text, and independently cross-checked against an official session-law reprint (a NACDL-hosted mirror of Iowa 2014 Chapter 1111); the current-Code section listing for chapter 708C was queried directly against legis.iowa.gov and returned zero sections. DNR park rule 571-61.10 and the Iowa DOT UAS webpage were each fetched and read in full directly from their official domains (legis.iowa.gov; iowadot.gov). Executive-order, AG-opinion, court-decision, procurement, and preemption negative findings reflect a research result (no source located in this pass), not a comprehensive negative-search confirmation.
notes: This is the single most important citation-correction finding for Iowa in this research pass: treat any secondary source's reference to 'Iowa Code §708C.1' as describing a 2014 bill provision that was never enacted, not current Iowa law. AEC firms should not rely on any secondary source's description of an Iowa state-agency UAV image-capture/reporting regime or a standalone Iowa UAV weaponization ban; no such current statute was located. Confirm any secondary-source Iowa UAS citation directly against legis.iowa.gov before relying on it.
